```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 08_hypothesis_testing_sample_z_score
title: >
  What if we had nine Spider-People?
questions:
  - id: nine_spider_z
    type: numeric
    prompt: >
      Suppose we had tested nine bitten kids instead of three, and their mean
      reaction time was still 189 milliseconds. Using the same population
      values, $\mu_0 = 284$ and $\sigma = 50$, what is the $z$-score for this
      sample mean?
    hints:
      - >
        The numerator hasn't changed: $M - \mu_0 = 189 - 284 = -95$.
      - >
        The standard error is now $\sigma_M = 50 / \sqrt{9}$.
    answer: -5.70
    tolerance: 0.02
    explanation: >
      $\sigma_M = 50 / \sqrt{9} = 16.67$, so $z = -95 / 16.67 = -5.70$. That's
      even farther into the lower tail than our sample of three, at
      $z = -3.29$.
    diagnostics:
      - id: nine_spider_se
        type: numeric
        prompt: What standard error did you calculate?
        answer: 16.67
        tolerance: 0.02
        explanation: >
          $\sigma_M = 50 / \sqrt{9} = 50 / 3 = 16.67$.

  - id: larger_sample_more_extreme
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      One kid at 189ms gave $z = -1.9$, three kids averaging 189ms gave
      $z = -3.29$, and nine kids averaging 189ms gave the answer above. Why does
      the same mean become more extreme as the sample gets bigger?
    options:
      - text: >
          The standard error gets smaller, so the same difference spans more
          standard errors.
        correct: true
      - text: >
          The difference between the sample mean and 284 gets bigger.
      - text: >
          The null hypothesis mean gets smaller.
      - text: >
          Larger samples have more sampling error.
    explanation: >
      The numerator, $189 - 284$, is the same every time. What changes is the
      denominator. Means of larger samples vary less from sample to sample, so
      the null distribution gets narrower, and a mean of 189 lands farther out
      in its tail.
```
